seo_title: Hurricane Damage Insurance: What Texas Policies Cover
meta_description: Hurricane damage insurance explained for Texas: wind vs. flood coverage, named storm deductibles, TWIA, and how to file and dispute a hurricane claim.
h1: Hurricane Damage Insurance: What You Need to Know in Texas
secondary_keywords: does homeowners insurance cover hurricane damage
excerpt: Hurricane damage insurance is really several coverages: wind, flood, and named storm deductibles. Learn what Texas policies cover, what they exclude, and how to handle a hurricane claim.
key_takeaways: Standard homeowners policies usually cover hurricane wind damage but exclude flood.
Flood coverage requires a separate policy, such as NFIP or private flood insurance.
Many coastal Texas homes need windstorm coverage through TWIA or a private carrier.
Named storm deductibles are often a percentage of dwelling coverage.
Document damage carefully and know your appraisal options if the payout is low.
body_html:
Hurricane damage insurance is not a single policy. In Texas, a standard homeowners policy usually covers hurricane wind damage, but flood and storm surge require separate flood insurance, and many coastal homes need windstorm coverage through TWIA. Most hurricane claims also carry a named storm or wind deductible based on a percentage of dwelling coverage.

Does homeowners insurance cover hurricane damage?

Partly. Most Texas homeowners policies cover damage caused by wind, including wind from a hurricane. If hurricane winds tear off shingles, break windows, or drive a tree through the roof, that damage is typically covered, subject to your deductible and policy terms.

What standard policies generally do not cover is flood. Water that rises from the ground, including storm surge and overflowing rivers or bayous, is excluded from almost every homeowners policy. That gap catches many Texans by surprise after a hurricane.

The cause of each piece of damage matters. Rain that enters through a wind-damaged roof is usually treated as wind damage. Water that flows in through the front door from flooded streets is flood damage. On many hurricane claims, both occur, and separating them becomes the main issue.

Because of that split, it helps to think of hurricane damage insurance as a set of coverages that must work together. Gaps between them, such as a home with wind coverage but no flood policy, are where most uninsured hurricane losses come from.

What does each type of coverage pay for?

Type of damageUsually covered byNotes
Wind damage to roof, siding, windowsHomeowners policy or windstorm policyCoastal homes may need TWIA or private wind coverage
Rain through wind-created openingsHomeowners or windstorm policyGenerally tied to the wind damage
Storm surge and rising waterFlood insuranceExcluded from standard homeowners policies
Fallen trees on the homeHomeowners policyDebris removal limits may apply
Additional living expensesHomeowners policy (Coverage D)If the home is uninhabitable from a covered loss
Code-required upgradesOrdinance or law coverageOften a separate, limited coverage

Code upgrades can be significant after a hurricane, especially for older homes. Learn more in ordinance and law coverage explained.

What is a hurricane or named storm deductible?

Many policies in hurricane-prone areas use a special deductible for named storms or for all wind and hail. Instead of a flat dollar amount, it is often a percentage of your dwelling coverage limit, commonly between 1% and 5%.

Here is an illustrative example. If your dwelling coverage is $300,000 and your named storm deductible is 2%, you would pay the first $6,000 of covered hurricane damage. At 5%, the deductible would be $15,000.

  • Check whether the deductible applies only to named storms or to all wind and hail.
  • Confirm whether it applies per storm or per season.
  • Note the dollar amount, not just the percentage, because it rises with your dwelling limit.
Tip: Review your declarations page before hurricane season begins on June 1. Knowing your deductible in dollars helps you plan for repairs and decide whether to adjust coverage at renewal.

Do you need flood insurance for hurricanes?

If you live anywhere a hurricane can bring heavy rain or storm surge, flood insurance is worth serious consideration. In Texas, that includes far more than beachfront property. Inland flooding from tropical rainfall has affected neighborhoods well away from the coast and outside mapped high-risk flood zones.

Flood coverage is available through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP), administered by FEMA, and through private flood insurers. Keep these points in mind:

  • NFIP policies generally have a 30-day waiting period before coverage takes effect, so you cannot wait until a storm is in the Gulf.
  • NFIP building and contents coverage have separate limits, and basement coverage is limited.
  • Private flood policies may offer higher limits or different terms; compare carefully.

How adjusters tell wind damage from flood damage

When both wind and water hit a home, adjusters look for clues. Water lines on interior walls, mud and debris deposits, and damage concentrated at lower levels point to flood. Missing shingles, broken windows, damaged soffits, and ceiling stains on upper floors point to wind and wind-driven rain.

Clear documentation helps you here. Photograph the roof and upper walls as well as the flood line, and note which rooms had ceiling leaks versus rising water. That evidence lets each policy pay for the damage it covers instead of leaving gaps between them.

Texas windstorm coverage and TWIA

In designated coastal counties, some homeowners policies exclude wind and hail. Property owners in those areas often buy windstorm coverage from the Texas Windstorm Insurance Association (TWIA), the state's insurer of last resort for wind and hail along the coast, or from a private carrier that offers wind coverage.

That means a single hurricane claim on the coast may involve three policies: a homeowners policy, a TWIA or private windstorm policy, and a flood policy. Each has its own deductible, claim process, and deadlines. TWIA policies follow their own claims and dispute procedures under Texas law, so read your TWIA policy carefully.

Coastal communities such as Galveston, Corpus Christi, and the Houston area face the greatest hurricane exposure, but strong storms can carry damaging winds well inland. Homeowners in our Houston service area and around Corpus Christi often deal with combined wind and water losses.

How much hurricane coverage do you need?

Review each coverage on your policy with hurricane risk in mind:

  1. Dwelling (Coverage A): enough to rebuild your home at current construction costs, not its market value.
  2. Other structures (Coverage B): fences, detached garages, and sheds, which are often damaged in hurricanes.
  3. Personal property (Coverage C): replacement cost coverage avoids heavy depreciation on contents.
  4. Loss of use (Coverage D): pays additional living expenses if you must move out during repairs.
  5. Ordinance or law: helps pay for code upgrades required during rebuilding.
  6. Flood: separate building and contents limits through NFIP or a private carrier.

Replacement cost versus actual cash value makes a big difference on roof and contents claims. Use our recoverable depreciation calculator to see how depreciation affects your payout. If you also face tornado risk, our guide on tornado damage insurance covers that peril.

How to file a hurricane damage insurance claim

After a hurricane, safety comes first. Once it is safe to return, follow these steps:

  1. Document everything. Photograph and video all damage, inside and out, before cleanup. Capture water lines on walls if flooding occurred.
  2. Prevent further damage. Tarp the roof, board up windows, and start drying out wet areas. Keep receipts for all materials and labor.
  3. Report the claim promptly. Notify every carrier that may be involved: homeowners, windstorm, and flood.
  4. Keep damaged items when possible. Adjusters may want to see them; if you must discard them, photograph them first.
  5. Make a contents inventory. List damaged belongings with descriptions, ages, and estimated values.
  6. Get a detailed estimate. A line-item estimate helps separate wind and flood damage and supports your claim.
  7. Track every deadline. Keep a log of calls, inspections, and letters.

Our free claim documentation checklist helps you organize photos and records. Texas Insurance Code Chapter 542 sets deadlines for insurers to acknowledge and decide claims, though they can be extended after a declared disaster. You can track key dates with our Texas claim deadline calculator.

Common hurricane claim disputes in Texas

Large storms produce thousands of claims at once, and adjusters may be brought in from out of state with limited knowledge of local construction and pricing. Hurricane claims frequently lead to disagreements, including:

  • Wind vs. flood: the carrier attributes damage to excluded flood rather than covered wind.
  • Underscoped roofs: partial repairs offered where the roof needs replacement.
  • Interior water damage: disputes over whether water entered through wind-created openings.
  • Pricing after a storm: estimates that do not reflect post-storm labor and material costs.
  • Code upgrades: required upgrades excluded or capped by policy limits.

When you and your carrier agree the damage is covered but disagree on how much it costs to repair, the appraisal clause found in most Texas homeowners policies offers a way to resolve the amount of loss without a lawsuit. Texas courts have held that appraisers may consider causation, such as how much damage the wind caused, but do not decide coverage. For many weather claims, Chapter 542A also requires 61 days' written notice before filing suit. This is general information, not legal advice; the Texas Department of Insurance offers additional consumer guidance.

Next steps to protect your home and your claim

Before hurricane season, review your homeowners, windstorm, and flood coverage, confirm your deductibles in dollars, and take dated photos of your home's condition. After a storm, document thoroughly and keep careful records.

Preparing your home before hurricane season

  • Trim trees and remove dead limbs near the house.
  • Secure or store outdoor furniture, grills, and other items that can become projectiles.
  • Inspect the roof, flashing, and gutters, and repair weak spots.
  • Store policy documents and your home inventory in the cloud or another safe place.
  • Know your evacuation route and plan for pets and medications.

Hurricane damage insurance works best when your coverage, records, and home are ready before a storm forms. A few hours of preparation in spring can save months of frustration in the fall.

faqs.q: Is storm surge covered by homeowners insurance in Texas?
faqs.a: Generally, no. Storm surge is treated as flood, which standard homeowners policies exclude. To cover surge and rising water, you need a separate flood policy through the NFIP or a private flood insurer. Wind damage from the same storm may still be covered by your homeowners or windstorm policy, subject to its deductible.

Property owners in designated Texas coastal counties whose homeowners policies exclude wind and hail often need separate windstorm coverage. TWIA provides that coverage when it is not available from private carriers, and eligibility requirements apply, including building code compliance for many structures. Ask your agent whether your policy covers wind or excludes it.

faqs.q: How long do I have to file a hurricane claim in Texas?
faqs.a: Deadlines depend on your policy. Many Texas policies require prompt notice and some set specific time limits for weather claims, and TWIA policies have their own filing deadlines. Report damage as soon as safely possible, then review each policy, including flood and windstorm coverage, for its notice and suit limitation requirements.

faqs.q: What if my insurer says hurricane damage was caused by flood, not wind?
faqs.a: Wind versus flood disputes are common after hurricanes. Gather photos, water line measurements, roof damage documentation, and weather data to show where wind caused damage. If both sides agree some wind damage is covered but disagree on the amount, appraisal may help resolve how much of the loss wind caused.

faqs.q: Does homeowners insurance pay for hotel stays after a hurricane?
faqs.a: If a covered loss makes your home uninhabitable, loss of use coverage, often called Coverage D or additional living expense, generally pays reasonable extra costs such as hotel stays and meals above your normal expenses. Keep every receipt. If the home is uninhabitable only because of flooding, coverage depends on your flood policy terms.
